title: POC Weekly Sync - Dedicated Sizing & Autoscale
summary: Weekly POC sync to review dedicated cluster sizing tests. Redwood presented updated throughput/latency numbers from the pilot run, recommended autoscale config (min=2, max=12, burst pool=3, cooldown 45s) and discussed warm-starting and prefix/KV cache benefits. Atlas asked about cost implications and failover to hosted models during peaks; agreed to run a 2-hour sustained burst test next week and exchange traffic profile and SOC2 docs.
transcript:
Header: 2025-06-16 15:00 UTC | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (CTO - Atlas), Priya Nair (SRE), Samir Patel (ML Eng)

[15:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — I see Jordan, Priya, Samir. Can you confirm?
[15:03] Jordan: Yep, here. Thanks Maya.
[15:04] Priya: Here. Sorry slight audio lag on my end.
[15:05] Maya: No worries. Quick agenda: review the week of load tests, discuss autoscale policy adjustments, burst handling and next steps. Luis will run the numbers, I'll call out action items.
[15:12] Luis: Alright, I pulled the 24-hour run we did on Thursday. Peak RPS was about 1,100 requests per sec for ~6 minutes during the synthetic spike, sustained baseline 220 RPS. P50 was 45ms, p95 across the cluster was 320ms for 1k tokens avg per call. We saw KV cache hit rates of ~48% for repeated prefixes which helped p50 a lot.
[15:18] Samir: Sorry can you repeat the p95 number? I missed that.
[15:19] Luis: Sure — p95 was ~320ms when autoscale hadn't fully ramped. Once extra workers came up, p95 dropped to ~200ms. There was a cold window of about 20-35 seconds for new pods.
[15:23] Priya: That cold window is our main concern. For Atlas we need predictable latency for transactional flows — p95 < 250ms ideally under typical spikes.
[15:27] Maya: Right. So our recommendation: min_replicas=2 to keep KV primed for baseline, target CPU or queue based scale up at 60% CPU or queue length ~80, max_replicas=12 to absorb larger events. Add a burst pool of 3 pre-warmed instances that can hand off fast for sub-minute spikes. Cooldown 45s to avoid flapping.
[15:31] Jordan: The burst pool — are those billed as reserved capacity or on-demand? How does that affect cost?
[15:33] Luis: Good question. For Dedicated the burst pool is reserved capacity that you can keep warm at lower unit cost than on-demand. It counts against committed capacity if you include it in your reserved contract; otherwise we offer short-term bursts billed at a premium. We can show cost delta in the spreadsheet.
[15:36] Samir: Also curious about fallback: if Dedicated is saturated, can we route overflow to Redwood hosted endpoints? We want to avoid request failures during growth.
[15:38] Maya: Yes, smart routing policy can route overflow to a hosted-compatible model. There are tradeoffs: data routing and residency — you'll need to confirm whether those requests can go to hosted or must stay inside your VPC.
[15:41] Priya: On that note, we still need the SOC2 docs and the SSO/SAML guide to present to compliance.
[15:43] Maya: We'll attach SOC2 and our security pack; Luis will include the SAML setup doc.
[15:45] Luis: Back to sizing — one thing we noticed is quantization profile impacts memory footprint and startup time. Using 4-bit quant with Redwood-verified kernels cuts memory by ~30% and reduced cold start time by ~10s in our runs. But quality regressed on a small subset of prompts — we flagged those in the eval.
[15:49] Samir: We saw that on our fin-text prompts too; some hallucination risk increased slightly. Can we pin model versions for the pilot to avoid surprises?
[15:51] Maya: Definitely; you can pin to the model+quantization profile. For the POC we recommend pinning to v1.3-4bit for size benefits, but we can run a quality sweep with your prompt set.
[15:56] Jordan: Operationally what's the warm-start procedure to reduce that 20-35s cold window? We can't afford long cold tails during business hours.
[15:58] Luis: Options: increase min_replicas, keep a burst pool of pre-warmed instances, and use prefix/KV caching to reduce time spent in early decoding. Also you can configure fast-start where we keep one instance with warmed model shards. There's a cost tradeoff.
[16:03] Priya: If we tune cooldown and lower scale threshold, do we risk oscillation? We don't want thrash.
[16:05] Luis: Correct — that's why we recommend hysteresis: a higher scale-down delay (cooldown 45-90s) and a small buffer on triggers so brief blips don't scale. We also recommend autoscale by queue length rather than raw CPU for LLM workloads.
[16:10] Samir: For the next test could we simulate our true traffic mix? The synthetic spike is okay but doesn't reflect burstiness of real user sessions.
[16:12] Maya: Yes — action item: Priya to share a 7-day anonymized traffic profile CSV. Luis will convert to load generator. We'll run a 2-hour sustained-burst test with that profile next Tuesday.
[16:16] Jordan: What pass/fail criteria do we want for go/no-go? I'd propose: sustained 900-1,200 RPS with p95 < 250ms, and no more than 2% error rate.
[16:18] Maya: That seems reasonable. We'll add cost targets too: under $X per 1M tokens — we'll calculate exact once we have traffic profile.
[16:21] Priya: Also, Samir, can you share which prompts triggered the quality regressions so we can vet?
[16:23] Samir: I'll upload the failing prompt list to the shared drive by EOD tomorrow.
[16:25] Luis: One more note: warm patching and kernel selection can be precompiled for your model family to shave a few seconds off start. We'll include a recommended compile profile.
[16:29] Jordan: Ok that's helpful. A couple quick asks: 1) send updated cost spreadsheet reflecting burst vs reserved; 2) SOC2 & SAML docs; 3) schedule the 2-hr burst run.
[16:31] Maya: We'll do that. We'll also propose an autoscale config to try: min=2, burst_pool=3 (pre-warmed), scale_metric=queue_length, scale_up_threshold=80, max=12, cooldown=45s.
[16:35] Priya: Sounds good. One last question — what happens during cloud provider preemption events? Do you have recommendations?
[16:36] Luis: For preemption we recommend multi-AZ placement and automatic fallback to smaller compatible model variants for brief periods. The runtime supports graceful degradation: switch to lower-quant or smaller model to keep tail latency low. We'll document the fallback chain.
[16:40] Maya: Great. Let's recap next steps and owners.
[16:41] Jordan: Thanks everyone.
[16:42] Maya: Thanks — we'll follow up with notes and scheduling.

Notes: occasional transcription errors present ("KV cash" instead of "KV cache" in some exports), speaker labels may shift slightly in extracted audio, timestamps approximate. Shared artifacts referenced: link:drive.re/redwood/atlas-poc-results (spreadsheet), link:drive.re/redwood/atlas-failing-prompts (prompt list).
